Many people sense that the part of Europe represented by Germany is dying through a terrible dysthanasia—a prolonged and agonizing death.
Few understand that the euthanasia of France and England belongs to the same process.
La France se meurt, ne troublez pas son agonie—France is dying; do not disturb its agony—Renan said sixty years ago.
Toynbee is fundamentally saying the same thing about England.

Today the Germans long for euthanasia and envy their Western neighbours the relative absence of pain in their dying. For the type of person devoted entirely to this world, dysthanasia is the great crime against humanity.
Anyone who grants a people euthanasia, by contrast, becomes a benefactor of humanity.
Hitler’s euthanasias were fraudulent, and were therefore crimes.

But his final political aim was to attach himself to the British Empire, to enter that distinguished firm, finally to become a great gentleman—in other words, to participate in the British agony and the British euthanasia.
To Hans Beyer, who wants to work on grace and law with reference to Nuremberg and thinks that the situation might be healed through “grace”:
The subject of grace and law is a great one.
I cannot properly connect it with Nuremberg so long as Nuremberg’s legal problems remain so monstrous. For the moment, Nuremberg belongs instead to the subject “grace and politics.”
And that is certainly a structural transformation of grace, something different from the kind of grace that can be related to law.
Then legality and the concept of the political; see 28 April 1948.
But I am no Ptolemaic man.
I turn no disc and am not myself turned.
To Herbert Nette, together with Konrad Weiß’s The Creature of the Word:
I am still occupied by your sentence that we use language as a vehicle in the same way that Black people drive cars or listen to the radio.
One could vary a sentence of Karl Marx in response:
The emancipation of Black people took place in such a way that white people became Black.
Again, great strength from Konrad Weiß, The Creature of the Word: the Tower of Babel of neutralizing linguistic unity.
“Even the confusion of languages is better today than this Babylonian unity.”
The κατέχων, the restrainer, can be recognized by the fact that he does not seek this world unity but instead lays down the imperial crown.
Making the imperial crown hereditary is naive. But the crown becomes hereditary through its connection with the practical power of a ruling house. And <can> a ruling house not itself be a κατέχων?
Then Konrad Weiß says of Theodor Haecker’s statements about language—which is, after all, something different from the word and has a stronger tendency toward neutralization:
“Haecker’s thought belongs to the Catholic literary movement, though it did not arise from that movement, because Haecker entered it as an outsider.
“He therefore did not pass through the earlier conflict within that movement between ‘classicist’ neutralization and ‘poetic’ realization.
“But now he too is struggling toward a specifically Catholic sharpening.

“The movement itself has in many cases—just as one can say of other intellectual and artistic decisions made by the older generation—turned, through its failure to bear fruit in creaturely and historical knowledge, from the word toward language, from the particular toward the universal, and from a neutralized form of life toward political confession.
“And now Haecker too is struggling for a genuine Catholic sharpening.”
That is the secret key phrase of my entire intellectual and public existence: the struggle for a genuinely Catholic sharpening of the issue.
Here, on this road toward Catholic sharpening, Theodor Haecker could no longer follow me.
Here they all fell away from me.
Only Konrad Weiß remained, and faithful friends such as Paul Adams.
First impression: language let completely loose; an extremely full-mouthed and wildly mixed vocabulary.
Is this the rhetorical ease of the Palatinate? Or is it an effect of Hitler and the Hitler Youth, which learned how to manipulate words?
Second impression: the need to find saviours and prophets and immediately greet them as such with loud enthusiasm. So he quickly turns Marshall, Toynbee, and Walter Lippmann into saviours.
Third impression: the young General Staff officer.
Danger of losing one’s dignity before people who simply do not want to be loved by us.
To Dr Wilhelm Schmitz, who sent me K. Schulte’s pamphlet and drew my attention to G. Radbruch’s favourable review of it in the SDJZ, April 1948:
Even poisonous mosquitoes such as Schulte have their meaning, or at least their function.
In Radbruch many things come together, not least an anti-Roman impulse that continues, unconsciously, to rumble around in the buried cellars of his emotional life.

A Holsteiner who has become a late Social Democrat—which means helpless—must find the unconstrained freedom of a man of Catholic stock opaque, meaning inaccessible to him, and therefore mythologize it into something Machiavellian and monstrous.
His fellow Holsteiner Ferdinand Tönnies, a Social Democrat of the old school, is of an entirely different calibre.
The direction in which my thoughts are moving after the first reading of Idea and Reality of the Free German Movement can best be indicated by the phrase pouvoir spirituel—spiritual power.
I know how irritating this expression must be to you. But I am not thinking of the long-established institutional forms that such a spiritual power has taken.
The whole of so-called nineteenth-century socialism was, in its original impulse, an attempt finally to create a spiritual power once again.

The first great document of socialism is not the Communist Manifesto of 1847, but Saint-Simon’s New Christianity of 1825, which explicitly proclaims the necessity and the goal of a new pouvoir spirituel.
The posthumously published second volume of Rudolf Sohm’s Church Law is a treasure house for every problem of constitutional and administrative law.
(Then more in the spirit of 1 May 1948: I saved the honour.)
Hobbes is the first modern thinker in whom hatred of ideologues becomes visible.

But wonderfully, this includes hatred of the ideologues of the right of resistance as well: the resistance ideologues who tyrannized us then just as they do today, who call upon others to commit sabotage while remaining safely out of range themselves, and who afterwards declare us criminals because we could not bring ourselves to become saboteurs.
In the case of Christianity, Hobbes takes them at their word: the only person obliged to die for his Christian faith is the person who preaches it. That is not so very far from Kierkegaard.
Kierkegaard would certainly have agreed with him enthusiastically.
A preacher of repentance such as Jaspers, who has not even been beaten up, does not deserve our interest.
Je faisais ce que faisait la magistrature—I did what the magistracy did.
The great problem of the right not to resist—the right of non-resistance.
The trial of Robert Brasillach became a procès d’opinion, a trial of opinion.
Jacques Isorni, Avocat à la Cour, published The Trial of Robert Brasillach with Flammarion in Paris in 1947.
On p. 167 comes the answer, to which the government prosecutor M. Reboul can reply only:
Il n’y a pas d’ordre légal—there is no legal order. And the authorities themselves committed sabotage as well.
To defend the old doctrine of non-resistance, which had been valid for four hundred years, now becomes a crime intellectuel—an intellectual crime.
The criminalization of aggressive war must go on reproducing itself and giving birth to ever new forms of criminalization.
The Diabolus ethicus, the ethical devil, stirred up the furor accusandi et persequendi—the frenzy of accusation and persecution.
There is a fine three-way dialogue between Robert Brasillach, the prosecutor M. Reboul, and the defence lawyer Jacques Isorni.
In the end, prosecutor and condemned man shake hands. But Brasillach is shot all the same.
Is the only thing that matters, then, the fact that the jury sentenced Brasillach to death and that the sentence was carried out?
What matters is that this discussion was published.
With us, people were—and still are—silenced.
I would gladly have died if my argument about the criminalization of aggressive war, written in August 1945, could have been published at the time or during the trials.
The intellectual struggle between the French republican and the fascist is impressive.
The defeated fascist is helpless, intellectually still embryonic. He finds no protection. But he still receives a public trial.
I think the passage describing the Republic as a whore was probably what emotionally tipped the jury toward a death sentence.
Le crime intellectuel: la trahison des clercs—the intellectual crime: the betrayal of the intellectuals.

“You were tearing apart a memory of yourselves, the memory we all share, the memory possessed by all of us intellectuals: the memory of the twenty-year-old student who, if he hungers for knowledge, can satisfy himself in France because every door to knowledge stands open to him and no tyranny closes any of them.”
It would be instructive to transfer these arguments and viewpoints to Germany.
Could anyone dare to say the equivalent to me?
The holders of licences issued in 1945 as heroes of free speech!
Radbruch as a member of the Resistance!
The greatness of present-day Germany: it talks about former colleagues who were silenced.
